1770-09-17-kyoto-cook.name: September 1770 storm (Kyoto red aurora / Cook's Endeavour aurora)
1770-09-17-kyoto-cook.context: Low-latitude aurorae were seen on almost nine consecutive nights (10-19 Sep 1770) from a sunspot group of up to ~6000 millionths of the solar hemisphere - about twice the Carrington group. It is the earliest known simultaneous auroral record from both hemispheres, and a Japanese chronicler in 1859 explicitly compared the Carrington aurora to it.
1770-09-17-kyoto-cook.effects: Pre-electrical era: no technology to disrupt, but the blood-red skies were recorded as alarming portents in 111 East Asian documents.

sightings.seen: Vivid red aurora with a fan of radial stripes and fine rays, extending toward the zenith around midnight on 17 Sep (painted in the manuscript 'Seikai' and described relative to the Milky Way in a diary).
Aurora on 17 Sep - the most equatorward sighting of the event at 18.8 deg MLAT.
Joseph Banks and Sydney Parkinson saw a red aurora australis 'reaching in height about twenty degrees above the horizon', ~22-24 local time on 16 Sep (-20.6 deg MLAT).

1847-10-24-greenwich.name: Great magnetic storm of 24 October 1847
1847-10-24-greenwich.context: One of the earliest great storms captured by a modern magnetic observatory; its Greenwich H-trace closely resembles the Colaba (Bombay) trace of the 1859 Carrington storm. Brilliant moonlight dimmed what Challis thought might otherwise have been the finest display ever seen in England.
1847-10-24-greenwich.effects: Greenwich's hand-read magnetometer recorded an H drop of ~1100 nT without going off scale. 1847 is also when British telegraph engineers (W. H. Barlow) first reported spontaneous currents in telegraph wires during auroras, though specific outages on 24 Oct were not found in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Glaisher reported 'a magnificent display' 21:57-22:04 UT, exactly when the magnetometer H-reading hit its minimum.
Challis saw an auroral corona: all streamers converging on a point at altitude ~70 deg, azimuth 18 deg E of S (near the magnetic zenith), despite bright moonlight.
Aurora borealis described in a contemporary Philosophical Magazine note 'as it was seen on Sunday evening, October 24, 1847'.

1859-08-29-carrington-precursor.name: First Carrington-period storm (28-29 August 1859)
1859-08-29-carrington-precursor.context: The first of a pair of superstorms from the same huge sunspot group (Carrington's group 520), launched while it was still far on the eastern side of the Sun. It pre-conditioned space so that the next CME, from the famous flare of 1 Sep, arrived unusually fast.
1859-08-29-carrington-precursor.effects: Telegraph operations were disrupted across North America and Europe on 28/29 Aug, a few days before the even larger 2 Sep storm.

sightings.seen: Whitish aurora seen 01:45-09:20 UT on 29 Aug, 'rising to the zenith' around 10:29-10:39 UT (34.0 deg MLAT).
Aurora seen low on the northern horizon (modelled ~7 deg elevation) around 03-04 local time (09:18-10:18 UT) - lowest visibility of this storm at 20.2 deg MLAT.
Intense display extending beyond the zenith and forming a corona on the night of 28 Aug.
Aurora australis reported in New Zealand newspapers mostly on 29 Aug.

1859-09-02-carrington.name: Carrington Event (1-2 September 1859)
1859-09-02-carrington.context: Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson saw the first recorded solar flare at 11:18 UT on 1 Sep; its CME hit Earth only ~17.5 h later, one of the fastest transits known. It is the benchmark 'worst case' storm for modern space-weather planning.
1859-09-02-carrington.effects: Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America: operators got shocks, sparks set telegraph paper on fire, and Boston-Portland operators unplugged their batteries and sent messages on auroral current alone. Rocky Mountain gold miners got up and made breakfast at 1 a.m., thinking dawn had come.

sightings.seen: Aurora australis 'invaded almost all the southern hemisphere of the sky', passing the zenith and covering ~1/3 of the sky, in red, pink, blue, yellow and white, ~01-05 local time on 2 Sep (~06-10 UT).
Aurora seen from the ship at -17.3 deg MLAT - the most equatorward confirmed visibility of the storm.
Red aurora up to 35 deg above the northern horizon, 00:30-01:30 local time on 2 Sep (~06 UT).
Aurora passed the zenith toward the northeast, with whitish and vivid red rays.
A beautiful stationary red arc passing through the zenith, with rays, drawn by Neumayer at 22:26 local time on 2 Sep.

1870-10-24-great-aurora.name: Great aurora of 24-25 October 1870 (double storm)
1870-10-24-great-aurora.context: A largely forgotten storm at the maximum of solar cycle 11, notable for green and white colours rather than the usual low-latitude red. A British observer wrote that it was '22 years since any approach to this grandeur has been seen'.
1870-10-24-great-aurora.effects: Telegraph communications were disrupted (letter by R. S. Culley, The Times, 31 Oct 1870), and magnetometers from Lisbon to Helsinki recorded two storms. The unusual display 'excited the fears of many' and filled European and American newspapers.

sightings.seen: Greenish arc low in the NW at 17:30 LT, then blood-red rays and masses of red light rising to the zenith with a corona phase, 18:00-20:30 LT on 24 Oct.
Red aurora with long rays shining in three parts of the sky on the evening of 24 Oct - a rare sight that impressed the population.
Aurora observed (33.4 deg MLAT).
Aurora seen on both 24 and 25 Oct - the lowest magnetic-latitude sighting (23.4 deg MLAT); also seen east to Baghdad.
'A brilliant display of the Aurora Australis' (Jones 1955).

1872-02-04-chapman-silverman.name: Chapman-Silverman storm (4 February 1872)
1872-02-04-chapman-silverman.context: Aurora was reported at 13 sites below 20 deg magnetic latitude (Bombay, Khartoum, Aden) - more than any other storm - making it one of the three largest storms on record, alongside 1859 and 1921. Remarkably, it came from a modest (~500 millionths) but complex sunspot group near disk centre.
1872-02-04-chapman-silverman.effects: Mediterranean submarine cables and the Lisbon-Gibraltar cables were badly disturbed, the London-Land's End line was cut off for hours, and the transatlantic cable was disrupted. Strong earth currents hit telegraphs in India and between Cairo and Khartoum, and the Havana magnetometer went off scale.

sightings.seen: A glowing arc spanning ~50 deg reaching very close to the zenith (overhead aurora), maximum ~17:54 UT, ending ~18:24 UT.
Sudden aurora at 18:56 UT shooting from the east horizon to the zenith; a dome-shaped bright blue light appeared below the zenith, then dissolved to deep violet.
A dark-red arch at 17:58 UT, then 16 steel-grey to silver-white bands reaching ~72 deg elevation, and a deep red glow along the horizon (19:25 UT).
Dark-red, very brilliant aurora extending halfway to the zenith, 19:00-21:30 local time (~23:00-01:30 UT).
Corona aurora overhead with rapidly changing rays; a sudden brightening at ~19:11 UT.

1882-11-17-great-aurora.name: Great Aurora / 'Electric Storm' of November 1882 (a.k.a. Transit of Venus storm)
1882-11-17-great-aurora.context: A giant naked-eye sunspot (up to 2,417 millionths of the hemisphere) was watched by soldiers marching to Queen Victoria's Hyde Park review, during the First International Polar Year and the dawn of Edison's electric lighting. Its 4-day average aa (214 nT, 17-20 Nov) is still the highest sustained disturbance since 1868.
1882-11-17-great-aurora.effects: Telegraph business east of the Mississippi and north of Washington came to a standstill; the Chicago Western Union switchboard caught fire several times and instruments melted, while Mexican, Cuban and transatlantic cables failed. Telephones rang spontaneously in France, Scottish railway signal bells rang by themselves, and a Milwaukee lamp was lit by 'volunteer' earth current.

sightings.seen: Red 'coronae borealis' with light streaming down from near the zenith and pale-green light fringing the London smoke cloud; at ~18:00 GMT on 17 Nov Maunder saw a 'magnificent streak of light' rise in the ENE and cross the sky just above the Moon in about two minutes (the famous 'auroral beam', also drawn by J. R. Capron at Guildown, Surrey, as a pearly-white/pale-green spindle).
Auroral streamers reaching the zenith - the lowest-latitude zenith (discrete) aurora identified for this storm (~45.5 deg geomagnetic latitude).
A rare aurora witnessed on 17 Nov by the new US Coast & Geodetic Survey magnetic observatory staff; the LA Times said the 'heavens presented a grand spectacle'.
Aurora reported (Monthly Weather Review 1882) - the southernmost US report, together with Galveston TX, Yuma AZ and San Diego CA; presumably low on the northern horizon (no elevation given).
Aurora seen as far south as Rome - the southernmost European report.

1903-10-31-halloween-1903.name: Extreme storm of 31 October 1903 ('the 1903 Halloween storm', solar-minimum superstorm)
1903-10-31-halloween-1903.context: Exactly a century before the 2003 Halloween storms, this superstorm struck just after solar minimum in the weak Solar Cycle 14, proving that a 'quiet' Sun can still unleash extreme events. It followed flares on 29-31 Oct from sunspot group 5098 and a ~1,500 km/s CME that arrived in ~27.5 h.
1903-10-31-halloween-1903.effects: Telegraphy in Spain and Portugal was interrupted 09:30-21:00 GMT (worst 12:30-15:00 GMT), Paris lost contact with North America and the Mediterranean, and London railway signalling and cables to Latin America, France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Algeria were disturbed. Chicago telephone lines carried ~675 V ('enough to kill a man'), Geneva's electric streetcars stopped, and 'practically the world's whole telegraph system was upset'.

sightings.seen: Aurora australis reported overhead (streamers reaching nearly to the zenith) on the evening of 31 Oct local time, used to reconstruct the oval edge at ~44.1 deg ILAT.
Aurora seen - the lowest-latitude southern report (-39.4 deg MLAT); presumably low on the southern horizon.
Aurora seen - the lowest magnetic-latitude northern report (40.9 deg MLAT).
Aurora reported overhead (47.9 deg MLAT) on the night of 31 Oct local time.

sightings.place: Yerkes Observatory, Williams Bay, Wisconsin, USA
sightings.seen: E. E. Barnard saw the aurora cover the whole sky (53.1 deg MLAT).

1907-02-09-february-1907.name: Magnetic storm and aurora of 9-10 February 1907
1907-02-09-february-1907.context: A short but sharp storm during the rise of Solar Cycle 14, when a sunspot near the centre of the disc was big enough to be seen with the naked eye through smoked glass. The aurora 'seems to have been widely observed on the evening of February 9' (Chree).
1907-02-09-february-1907.effects: At Kew the horizontal force fell more than 355 nT in 8 minutes (20:25-20:33 GMT) and the trace ran off the recording sheet; the total range exceeded 480 nT - the largest storm at Kew since 31 Oct 1903. No specific technology impacts were found in the sources used.

sightings.seen: Unusually beautiful display 18:30-23:00 GMT, best 20:00-21:30: brilliant soft-white light tinged pale green filling the NW and N sky, curved wavy bands rushing up to the zenith and hanging there as white cloudy patches, with a dull faint red around Ursa Major and Leo.
Green 'streaks of light' seen at the zenith - the lowest-latitude zenith (discrete) aurora identified for this storm (48.6 deg geomagnetic latitude).

1909-09-25-september-1909.name: Great magnetic storm of 25 September 1909
1909-09-25-september-1909.context: Driven by a >=X10-class flare on 24 Sep from sunspot group 6728 and a ~1,700 km/s CME, it was one of the most intense storms of the 20th century and about as strong as the March 1989 Quebec storm. It produced the largest magnetic range in Greenwich records for 1859-1954 (1,710 nT), in the weak Solar Cycle 14.
1909-09-25-september-1909.effects: Telegraph and cable systems worldwide were disrupted from the storm's onset: New York telegraph lines carried >500 V, lighting lamps and throwing sparks across open keys, and Tokyo recorded >110 V between Tokyo and Yokkaichi at 13:35 UT, with the Tokyo-Ogasawara-Guam cable also affected. Western Australian telegraph lines had to be worked with their batteries cut out for half an hour.

sightings.seen: Red aurora in the north reaching ~30 deg above the horizon, ~16:40-16:57 UT near the Dst minimum - the lowest-MLAT credible sighting (23.2 deg MLAT).
Aurora in the north that began bluish-white and turned red (sunlit aurora giving way to the usual low-latitude red aurora), ~14:30-15:55 UT (31.8 deg MLAT).

Pale opalescent glow in the south with bright ribbons running up nearly to the zenith, rays rising from a dark arch (12-14 UT), then around midnight local (~14 UT) a red glow so bright many thought it was a fire.

From ~13 UT a white glow in the south with arches and columns of white light, greenish clouds, then pink deepening to carmine 'till the sky was a restless sea of blood-red fire'; renewed brilliance near 16 UT and again before dawn.
Despite bright moonlight, 'a lovely rose-pink blush overspreading the sky', strongest on the southern horizon and extending to and beyond the zenith, with pulsations (~18:00-18:40 UT).

1919-08-11-august-1919.name: Magnetic storm of 11-12 August 1919
1919-08-11-august-1919.context: A borderline 'great' storm in the declining phase of Solar Cycle 15, less than two years before the May 1921 superstorm.
1919-08-11-august-1919.effects: Serious disturbances on telegraph lines throughout Western Australia; at Watheroo the H-trace ran off the recording sheet (range >378 nT) and the storm was the most violent recorded at some observatories since September 1909.

sightings.seen: Green auroral streamers at the zenith - the lowest-latitude zenith (discrete) aurora identified for this storm (46.9 deg geomagnetic latitude).
Aurora seen on the night of 11 August (Watheroo Observatory letter); no details of form or elevation.
The lowest-latitude sighting listed by Silverman (2006) for this storm (elevation unspecified).

1920-03-23-march-1920.name: Great aurora and magnetic storm of 22-23 March 1920
1920-03-23-march-1920.context: Near-maximum of Solar Cycle 15, a year before the May 1921 superstorm; a 'great aurora' was noted in Boston, Washington and Norway, and Stormer's multi-station photography that night was used to measure auroral heights.
1920-03-23-march-1920.effects: The storm's range was so large that the Cheltenham variometer magnet was driven beyond stable equilibrium and stopped recording shortly before 03 GMT on 23 Mar, and parts of other US Coast & Geodetic Survey records were lost. No specific telegraph or grid impacts were confirmed in the sources used.

sightings.seen: Rays rising from a bright band low in the north at 01:05-01:10 GMT (8:05 pm EST) with a rosy ray in the east; from ~03:00 GMT rays on a grand scale converged to a corona near Saturn south of the zenith, a rosy glow in the west, and by ~03:40 GMT nearly the entire sky was lit.

Carl Stormer found the auroral arc in the SOUTH (below Sirius) at dusk, then photographed coronas all night: yellow-red in the evening, later greenish, and a remarkable corona of long blue rays at ~03:40-03:46 GMT on 23 Mar.
Thin white lines of aurora at the zenith - the lowest-latitude zenith (discrete) aurora identified for this storm (43.0 deg geomagnetic latitude).
Aurora observed from 9 pm to 3 am local time (~13:00-19:00 GMT on 22 Mar); also seen along the south coast to Adelaide.
Aurora seen - the lowest-latitude Australian report, with a faint display at Perth around 3 am local (~19 GMT).

1921-05-15-new-york-railroad-storm.name: New York Railroad Storm (great storm of 13-16 May 1921)
1921-05-15-new-york-railroad-storm.context: A series of CMEs from a huge near-equatorial sunspot group (1,709 millionths) in the declining phase of Solar Cycle 15 compressed the magnetosphere to ~5.3 Earth radii; the storm rivals the 1859 Carrington event. It is the benchmark worst case for modern power-grid planning.
1921-05-15-new-york-railroad-storm.effects: Induced currents set fire to the Central New England Railroad station at Brewster, NY (~03-04 GMT on 15 May), destroyed the Karlstad telephone exchange in Sweden, blew fuses and knocked out Brooklyn-Long Island phone lines, and put >1,000 V on US telegraph wires; transatlantic cables and radio were also disrupted. The New York Central signal failure and 57th Street tower fire (11:04 GMT) that gave the storm its name may have been a coincidental fault (Hapgood 2019).

sightings.seen: Red aurora up to 22 deg elevation in the southern sky 05:45-06:30 GMT on 15 May (18:15-19:00 local), most intense ~06:20 GMT, moving east to west with a yellow streamer - reported by professional observers at only ~13-16 deg magnetic latitude.
Golden-yellow 'bars of light' at the zenith - the lowest-latitude zenith (discrete) aurora identified for this storm (29.7 deg geomagnetic latitude).

An auroral arc overhead like a 'curtain flapping in the wind' ~02:30-05:00 GMT on 15 May, so bright that 'the intense lights of the electric signs along Broadway could not dim the brilliance of the flaring skies'.
Bright aurora from 20:30 local time until daylight (~03:30-10:30 GMT on 15 May), fading at 22:30 then reviving, and still active on the northern horizon at 03:30 local.
Bernard Lyot watched the aurora 00:20-03:05 GMT on 15 May with maxima at 01:14, 02:10 and 03:05; the 02:10 peak hid 2nd-magnitude stars and was bright enough to read a watch.

1928-07-08-july-1928.name: July 1928 storm
1928-07-08-july-1928.context: The most intense storm of solar cycle 16 and a short, violent 'first magnitude' storm of only ~12 hours. It predates the Kp index (1932), so its size is known only from later reconstructions of observatory records.
1928-07-08-july-1928.effects: Serious interference with telegraph and telephone transmission in the USA; newspapers of 8 July reported telegraph lines 'tied up' by the aurora. Cheltenham recorded a horizontal-intensity range of more than 1270 nT (instrument partly off scale).

sightings.seen: White and pink auroral beams reaching the zenith (Santa Fe New Mexican, via Love et al. 2025).
'A fine display of aurora' observed by U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey staff during the storm night of 7-8 July (Hartnell 1928).

1938-01-22-january-1938-first-twin.name: January 1938 storms (first twin, 21-22 Jan)
1938-01-22-january-1938-first-twin.context: The first of the 'twin' great storms of January 1938, both driven by the giant sunspot group RGO 12673 (7th largest of 1874-1954). It was best seen around the Pacific (Japan, Sakhalin, Australia, western and central USA) because the peak fell in their night.
1938-01-22-january-1938-first-twin.effects: Aurorae across the USSR were accompanied by interruptions of radio and telegraph communications. A complete short-wave blackout was reported in the polar region 16-19 January 1938, probably from a solar proton event.

sightings.seen: Aurora low in the northern sky (est. up to ~20 deg elevation) at 19:30-19:45 local (~10:30 UT); the lowest-MLAT sighting (29.5 deg) of the Jan 1938 sequence.
Aurora reported (nearly) overhead 18:30-20:30 local (~09:30-11:30 UT); used by Hayakawa et al. to put the oval edge at 40.3 deg ILAT.
Drawing at 19:25 local shows a red background with yellow streaks and continual pulsation of the light.
Aurora australis reported around 22:00 local on the 22nd (~10:30 UT); the southern display was brightest this night in Australia/NZ.
Red and white streamers, curtains and beams described as reaching 'beyond the zenith' (Los Angeles Times, via Love et al. 2025).

1938-01-25-fatima-storm.name: Fatima Storm / Great Aurora of 25-26 January 1938
1938-01-25-fatima-storm.context: Seen across all of Europe - the widest auroral visibility there in generations - the crimson display was read by many as an omen of war. Sister Lucia of Fatima identified it as the 'night illumined by an unknown light' she said had been foretold in 1917 as a sign before a greater war, hence its name.
1938-01-25-fatima-storm.effects: Short-wave radio was shut down for about 12 h in Canada, Western Union teletype circuits in New York malfunctioned and railway signalling between Manchester and Sheffield failed. Fire brigades were called out across Europe (Windsor Castle guards summoned one), as people mistook the red sky for great fires.

sightings.seen: Aurora rising up to ~45 deg above the northern horizon, 22:10-23:00 local (~20:10-21:00 UT); used to put the oval edge at 40.0 deg ILAT.
Aurora seen 20:00-21:22 local over French North Africa (39.6 deg MLAT), along with reports from Sicily, Gibraltar, Portugal and Morocco/Tunisia.
Crimson arches with green and blue-white radiating from a corona near the zenith; residents called the fire brigade thinking the town was ablaze.
Red aurora seen in the northern sky (43.8 deg MLAT); fire alarms were also raised there and in San Diego.
Brief aurora australis logged at ~00:15 ship time on 26 Jan (~23:15 UT 25 Jan, at the storm peak) - the lowest-latitude sighting of the storm (-29.9 deg MLAT).

1938-04-16-april-1938.name: April 1938 storm
1938-04-16-april-1938.context: A short, sharp storm three months after the Fatima aurora, during the maximum of solar cycle 17. Its Dst was modest (about -255 nT), but its Kp reached the top value of 9 and discrete aurora was seen overhead in southern California.
1938-04-16-april-1938.effects: Telegraph problems were reported in Norway, and compass bearings were thrown off by about 5.5 deg. Newspapers called it the most powerful magnetic storm since the previous summer.

sightings.seen: Red auroral streamers seen overhead at the zenith on the night of 15-16 April local time (Long Beach Sun, via Love et al. 2025).

1940-03-24-easter-sunday-storm.name: Easter Sunday Storm (March 1940)
1940-03-24-easter-sunday-storm.context: Struck on Easter Sunday during the 'Phoney War' months of WWII, from an X-class-level flare (est. ~X35) on 23 March; its sudden commencement was one of the largest ever recorded. Geoelectric voltages on some lines exceeded what the March 1989 storm would have induced.
1940-03-24-easter-sunday-storm.effects: Widespread interference on US and Canadian long lines in daytime: nearly all overseas radiotelephone circuits and ship services were interrupted, AP's 10,000-mile wirephoto network went down, telegraph lines were 'paralysed' and up to ~800 V was induced on a Boston-Keene telephone line. Power systems saw voltage dips up to 10%, tripped transformer banks and blown fuses - one of the first well-documented grid impacts.

sightings.seen: Rising orange shafts with a thin white-yellow cloud, up to ~20 deg high, 17:30-19:30 UT; aurora was reported across Greece from Thrace to Crete and in Turkey.
A Japanese vessel saw a glow likened to the light just before sunrise, 17:57-18:05 and 18:35-18:39 UT (31.2 deg MLAT).
Aurora borealis reported during the night (29.7 deg MLAT), probably only a few degrees above the northern horizon.
Aurora australis seen 17-20 UT, during the storm main phase.
Green vertical streamers overhead (Cleveland Plain Dealer, via Love et al. 2025) - American viewing was hampered by the near-full Moon.

1941-03-01-march-1941.name: March 1941 superstorm
1941-03-01-march-1941.context: The first of three extreme storms in 1941 (4th, 12th and 5th largest in the aa index 1868-2010), driven by an unusually fast CME (~2260 km/s, 4th fastest known transit). With wartime blackouts in Europe, the best records come from Japan and Manchuria.
1941-03-01-march-1941.effects: Three of the four Dst-station magnetograms went off scale; Greenwich-Abinger recorded its 3rd-largest disturbance range of 1874-1954 (~1650-1710 nT). A telegraph disturbance was reported at Oshidomari at 16:55-17:05 UT, and a 4-day polar-cap radio absorption event preceded the storm.

sightings.seen: Reddish glow drifting from NW to E, then reddish glow with stripes moving NE to NW, 15:05-16:18 and 17:40-18:20 UT (37.8 deg MLAT).
Diffuse red aurora 13:56-19:30 UT that at its maximum rose almost to the zenith (35.2 deg MLAT) - possibly partly a SAR arc.
Red-yellow glow with bluish-white stripes up to 60-70 deg elevation, 16:05-18:30 UT; sketched by observers (35.0 deg MLAT).
Red and white shafts of light reaching the zenith (West Australian, via Love et al. 2025).

1941-07-05-july-1941.name: July 1941 storm (Fourth of July storm)
1941-07-05-july-1941.context: The second of 1941's three extreme storms (12th largest in aa 1868-2010) and the second most intense of solar cycle 17. It peaked on the night of the US Independence Day holiday, with overhead aurora on the southern California coast.
1941-07-05-july-1941.effects: Newspapers on 6 July reported that sunspots had 'silenced' short-wave radio and that the magnetic storm upset communication lines.

sightings.seen: Pink auroral curtain at the zenith on the night of 4-5 July local time (Santa Barbara News-Press, via Love et al. 2025).

1941-09-18-geomagnetic-blitz.name: Geomagnetic Blitz of September 1941
1941-09-18-geomagnetic-blitz.context: With a nearly new Moon, millions of Americans saw the brightest aurora in decades while the US was not yet in WWII; some feared it was a wartime signal. Mid-Atlantic, the light exposed convoy SC-44 to a U-boat wolf pack, and HMCS Levis was sunk with 18 killed.
1941-09-18-geomagnetic-blitz.effects: Uncontrolled voltage swings hit Pennsylvania Water and Power lines to Baltimore and Washington at 19:45-19:50 UT on 18 Sep, and transformers 'groaned'. Radio broadcasts failed - a Dodgers-Pirates game went silent for ~15 minutes - and a station's program mixed with overheard phone calls; transatlantic short-wave was disrupted all day.

sightings.seen: Brilliant rays and moving drapery of pink, green and lavender, with an auroral corona overhead - rare at mid-continental latitudes.

sightings.place: North Atlantic east of Cape Farewell (U-74 / HMCS Levis)
sightings.seen: Aurora so bright ('as bright as day') that U-boat U-74 could see and torpedo the Canadian corvette HMCS Levis at ~05:03 UT on 19 Sep.
Accounts of the display received from Pasadena; Weather Bureau observers also reported aurora in New Mexico.
Searchlight-like beams and a mauve glow reaching the zenith (Daily Advertiser, Wagga Wagga, via Love et al. 2025).

1946-03-28-march-1946-superstorm.name: March 1946 superstorm
1946-03-28-march-1946-superstorm.context: The largest storm of solar cycle 18 and one of only a handful of known 'superstorms' (Dst <= -500 nT), comparable with March 1989. A fast CME (~1590 km/s) from a major flare at ~04:10-04:45 GMT on 27 March reached Earth only ~26 hours later.
1946-03-28-march-1946-superstorm.effects: At Abinger (UK), long-distance radio channels and submarine-cable telegraphy were dislocated. In Ontario, Canada, the Port Arthur transformer tripped six times and the Crow River transformer twice between 11:46 and 12:17 UT as the main phase began.

sightings.seen: Aurora from 11:35 to at least 14:15 UT; at 13:30 UT very bright rays appeared 10 deg north of the zenith and a corona extended beyond the zenith.

sightings.place: Broken Hill, New South Wales, Australia
sightings.seen: Red, green, blue and yellow rays reaching the zenith (Barrier Miner, via Love et al. 2025).
'Strong aurora, extending over the zenith' from sunset to about 20 UT, during the early recovery phase.

1949-01-26-january-1949.name: January 1949 storm
1949-01-26-january-1949.context: The second most intense storm of solar cycle 18, in two steps: a first dip on 25 Jan and a deeper one around 00 UT on 26 Jan. Its auroral records are sparse compared with the 1938-1946 storms.
1949-01-26-january-1949.effects: A radio disturbance attributed to a very large sunspot was reported in the New York Times of 28 January 1949. No infrastructure impacts were found in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Blue, green and red 'fingers', 'spears' and rays overhead (Bend Bulletin, via Love et al. 2025).
A 'picket fence' of light (Scottsbluff Star-Herald) - either discrete aurora or a STEVE-like sub-auroral feature.

1957-09-05-early-september-1957.name: Early-September 1957 storm (IGY)
1957-09-05-early-september-1957.context: The first of three Dst <= -300 nT storms in September 1957, the most eruptive month of Solar Cycle 19 (the strongest sunspot cycle on record), two months into the International Geophysical Year.
1957-09-05-early-september-1957.effects: No specific grid or cable failures were found for this storm in the sources consulted; its main recorded social footprint was a wave of Midwest UFO reports that the US Air Force attributed to the aurora.

sightings.seen: Ground Observer Corps UFO report at 21:27 local on 4 Sep: a stationary 'circle of light with streaks' in red, white, orange and green, blinking and fading for 21 min; USAF Project Blue Book identified it as the aurora seen across the Midwest [dipole MLAT +50.9°]
Auroral rays seen at the zenith (overhead), per local newspaper report compiled by Love et al. (2025) [dipole MLAT +51.0°]
'Aurora borealis stages sky show in Chicago area' (Chicago Daily Tribune, 5 Sep 1957, front page) [dipole MLAT +52.7°]
Second Project Blue Book 'object' on the same night, likewise attributed to aurora [dipole MLAT +55.3°]

1957-09-13-september-1957-superstorm.name: Great storm of 13 September 1957 (IGY)
1957-09-13-september-1957-superstorm.context: The third-largest storm in the Kyoto Dst record (since 1957). It arrived during the IGY, when hundreds of volunteer auroral observers in Australia and New Zealand had been alerted in advance and cameras filmed the display.
1957-09-13-september-1957-superstorm.effects: Long-distance radio circuits at New Zealand's Makara station could not be kept open for more than a minute or so at the height of the aurora. Hard-copy engineering impacts are otherwise poorly documented.

sightings.seen: Auroral streaks at the zenith in red, yellow and white (Fresno Bee, via Love et al. 2025); the Los Angeles Times reported a 'rare northern lights display in southland' the same night [dipole MLAT +43.4°]
Reddish aurora with orange components up to 38° elevation in the north, 18:30-22:05 JST (09:30-13:05 UT); lowest-MLAT Japanese site, used to put the oval boundary at 38.3° ILAT [dipole MLAT +31.9°]

'One of the most brilliant displays': long pink streamers arched across the sky 'like the spokes of a wheel' centred north of the city (a corona), green on the southern horizon; peaks ~20:00 and ~23:00 NZST (08 and 11 UT) [dipole MLAT -50.7°]
Changing curtains of deep rose-pink almost to the zenith in the south-west over lemon and green, best ~20:30 NZST (08:30 UT); thousands went outdoors [dipole MLAT -45.4°]
Aurora australis reported 'as far north as Mackay'; IGY reporter F. Jacka described a greenish arc in the south and a reddish arc from north-east to north-west [dipole MLAT -30.0°]

1957-09-23-late-september-1957.name: Late-September 1957 storm (IGY)
1957-09-23-late-september-1957.context: A multi-day storm sequence (21-24 Sep) and the third Dst <= -300 nT storm within three weeks. It came just days before Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 Oct 1957.
1957-09-23-late-september-1957.effects: Natural Resources Canada lists a power-system breaker trip on 22 Sep 1957 caused by transformer core saturation and excessive harmonic currents in ground relays.

sightings.seen: 'Shafts of light' at the zenith in orange, red, pink, purple and white (Kansas City Times, via Love et al. 2025) [dipole MLAT +49.3°]
'Aurora lights northern sky in city region' (Chicago Daily Tribune, 23 Sep 1957) [dipole MLAT +52.7°]
Aurora australis reported on the night of 22/23 Sep and early morning (Carter Observatory) [dipole MLAT -51.6°]
Aurora reported to Carter Observatory the same night; Wellington was clouded out [dipole MLAT -47.5°]
Aurora reported to Carter Observatory the same night [dipole MLAT -46.3°]

1958-02-11-igy-great-storm.name: Great IGY storm of 11 February 1958
1958-02-11-igy-great-storm.context: The fourth-largest storm in the Kyoto Dst record and the signature space-weather event of the International Geophysical Year. New York Times reporter Walter Sullivan chronicled it almost minute-by-minute, and Europeans reportedly thought cities were on fire.
1958-02-11-igy-great-storm.effects: Circuit breakers tripped in Ontario, briefly blacking out the Toronto area; the new TAT-1 transatlantic telephone cable saw ~2.6 kV swings that made voice traffic unintelligible, and AT&T lines in Utah carried up to 130 V. Worldwide HF radio was blacked out (US-Europe traffic was rerouted via South America and Africa), and NZ-Australia cable circuits were unusable for hours.

sightings.seen: Aurora reported down to Mexico City (Rivera-Terrazas & González 1964; Sullivan 1961); the lowest-MLAT confirmed site in the American sector [dipole MLAT +29.3°]
Red aurora 'suddenly seen' on the evening of 10 Feb local (early 11 Feb UT), along with Los Angeles, Washington and New York [dipole MLAT +34.3°]
A red auroral 'sheet' at the zenith (Fresno Bee, via Love et al. 2025); in California's San Joaquin Valley red aurora was watched 21:50-02:40 EST (02:50-07:40 UT) [dipole MLAT +43.4°]
Dark-red glow with fan-shaped white/yellowish pillars up to ~60° elevation, peak 10:30-10:50 UT; Japan's first photographed aurora ('like a mountain fire far away') [dipole MLAT +34.0°]
Streamers of red, pink and green moving from the horizon to the zenith; seen across NZ from Kaitaia to Invercargill, 20:45 NZST to ~02:00 (08:45-14:00 UT) [dipole MLAT -50.7°]

1958-07-08-july-1958.name: July 1958 storm (IGY)
1958-07-08-july-1958.context: Followed an intense solar flare on 7 July 1958 that was reported from Australia, Japan and Hawaii during an IGY 'special world interval' of intensified observation.
1958-07-08-july-1958.effects: New Zealand's Post Office called it the worst radio fade-out in years: from midnight 8/9 Jul all long-distance HF contact with Australia, Vancouver, Singapore and Apia was lost, and Harewood had a complete short-wave blackout.

sightings.seen: 'A spectacular aurora' in the southern sky on the night of 8 Jul NZST [dipole MLAT -51.6°]

At 20:00 NZST 9 Jul (08 UT) a red shaft of light in the south flanked by a rosy-pink glow and faint bluish-white radiating shafts, fading about an hour later; the best of several auroras that year [dipole MLAT -48.0°]

1958-09-04-september-1958.name: September 1958 storm (IGY)
1958-09-04-september-1958.context: One of 14 storms with Dst <= -250 nT in Solar Cycle 19, near the end of the IGY. A Spanish-language press review also notes auroras seen in northern Germany around 4-5 Sep 1958.
1958-09-04-september-1958.effects: No technological impacts were found in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Auroral 'banners' and a 'canopy' (corona) at the zenith (Maffitt 1958, via Love et al. 2025) [dipole MLAT +50.1°]

1959-07-15-july-1959.name: Great storm of 15 July 1959
1959-07-15-july-1959.context: The second-largest storm since the IGY by Dst. It was driven by a CME from a giant flare on 14 July that crossed to Earth in ~28 h (~1460 km/s), and was part of the extreme July 1959 solar-particle episode.
1959-07-15-july-1959.effects: Short- and medium-wave contact at Tashkent was completely suspended 15:00-17:30 UT; the BBC could not be heard in NZ after 01:00, and London press messages had to be rerouted by cable, taking over seven hours.

sightings.seen: 'Six columns of white light' near the zenith with red, pink, greenish and orange-yellow colours, 13:58-18:31 UT [dipole MLAT +36.5°]
Predominantly dark-red aurora with occasional curtains up to ~30° elevation, 18:20-18:55 UT; the lowest-MLAT sighting (27.4°) [dipole MLAT +27.4°]
Aurora seen 22:10-00:20 local time despite the bright summer night (also reported from Sverdlovsk) [dipole MLAT +47.2°]
Red glow covering up to half the sky from midnight to 06:00 NZST on 16 Jul (12-18 UT 15 Jul), pulsing and 'dancing'; called the century's longest, most brilliant aurora australis [dipole MLAT -41.1°]
Aurora watched at NZ's northern tip the same night [dipole MLAT -39.1°]

1960-04-01-april-1960.name: Storm of 31 March - 1 April 1960
1960-04-01-april-1960.context: A long, intense storm: daily Ap 241 on 1 Apr 1960 is the fourth-highest daily Ap since 1932. It came during the declining phase of Solar Cycle 19.
1960-04-01-april-1960.effects: In Southland (NZ) induced earth currents disrupted Invercargill-Bluff toll circuits, rang home telephones and triggered a false fire alarm; Awarua Radio lost all contact with Scott Base (Antarctica), Macquarie Island, Milford Sound and Haast.

sightings.seen: Auroral streamers at the zenith (via Love et al. 2025) [dipole MLAT +49.4°]
'Aurora borealis viewed here' (Washington Post, 1 Apr 1960, front page) [dipole MLAT +50.3°]
'One of the most intense auroras in recent years' on the night of 1 Apr NZST; its ground currents rang telephones and set off the Bluff fire alarm at 00:10 (12:10 UT) [dipole MLAT -51.7°]

1960-04-30-late-april-1960.name: Storm of 30 April 1960
1960-04-30-late-april-1960.context: A short, sharp storm one month after the April 1 event, with Kp 9o at 15-18 UT. Its main phase fell in daylight over the Americas and around dawn in Australasia, which may explain why no auroral reports were found.
1960-04-30-late-april-1960.effects: No documented impacts were found in the sources consulted.

1960-11-13-november-1960.name: Great storm of 12-13 November 1960
1960-11-13-november-1960.context: Daily Ap reached 280 on 13 Nov 1960, the highest daily Ap in the GFZ record since 1932. The storm was part of a flare sequence (12 and 15 Nov) that also produced one of the largest solar-proton events of the era.
1960-11-13-november-1960.effects: Sweden's power system had 30 line circuit breakers trip, and power-feed circuits on transatlantic cables were disturbed. Global radio communications were disrupted.

sightings.seen: Auroral streaks at the zenith (Evening Republican, via Love et al. 2025) [dipole MLAT +50.1°]
'Aurora borealis proves thriller' and 'lights up D.C. area', with callers jamming switchboards (Washington Post, 13 Nov 1960) [dipole MLAT +50.3°]
Red, orange and green lights; Morehead Planetarium called it 'a rare treat. We don't get it often at this latitude' [dipole MLAT +47.2°]
'Display of northern lights here creates glow' (New York Times, 13 Nov 1960) [dipole MLAT +52.2°]

1967-05-26-may-1967-great-storm.name: Great storm of May 1967 (Cold War radar-jamming scare)
1967-05-26-may-1967-great-storm.context: Knipp et al. (2016) showed that the storm nearly became a Cold War flashpoint and led directly to the build-up of US military space-weather forecasting. It is the eighth-largest Dst storm on record.
1967-05-26-may-1967-great-storm.effects: On 23 May a record solar radio burst 'jammed' all three BMEWS missile-warning radars. Commanders suspected Soviet jamming and readied nuclear-armed bombers until USAF solar forecasters identified the Sun as the cause. The storm then disrupted HF and polar radio, degraded satellite tracking through extreme atmospheric drag, and pushed the magnetopause inside geosynchronous orbit.

sightings.seen: Red auroral rays at the zenith (Delta Democrat-Times, via Love et al. 2025) [dipole MLAT +42.7°]
Aurora reported as far south as New Mexico, ~32°N near the US-Mexico border (Castelli et al. 1968); point is representative, the exact site is not given [dipole MLAT +41.2°]
Aurora overhead; 'City gets rare look at northern lights' (Washington Post, 27 May 1967) [dipole MLAT +50.2°]
Class II aurora (Findlay et al. 1969), also seen in central Europe; point is representative (Exeter) [dipole MLAT +54.0°]

1972-08-04-august-1972.name: August 1972 storm (ultra-fast CME; Vietnam sea-mine storm)
1972-08-04-august-1972.context: The CME crossed from Sun to Earth in a record 14.6 h (~2,850 km/s) and struck at 20:54 UT, compressing the magnetopause to ~5 Earth radii. The ring current never grew large (Dst only -125 nT) because the cloud's field turned northward, so this 'Carrington-class' event produced relatively modest low-latitude aurora. It fell between Apollo 16 and Apollo 17.
1972-08-04-august-1972.effects: Dozens of US Navy magnetic sea mines off Hai Phong, North Vietnam, detonated within ~30 s on 4 Aug. AT&T's L4 coaxial cable (Illinois-Iowa) failed under a 7 V/km induced field at 22:40 UT; North American utilities saw voltage swings and transformer trips, and Manitoba Hydro exports fell 120 MW in minutes. An INTELSAT IV array lost ~5% power, a DSCS II satellite failed, and the SEP flux would have endangered any Apollo crew on a moonwalk.

sightings.seen: Within ~15 min of the 22:38 UT impulse, the first glow of a spectacular aurora bright enough to cast shadows (Taylor & Howarth 1972; ~54° MLAT); point is representative [dipole MLAT +53.6°]
Within ~2 h commercial pilots reported aurora as far south as Bilbao (~46° MLAT) [dipole MLAT +46.6°]

1981-04-13-sts1-red-aurora.name: April 1981 storm (the 'Shuttle red aurora')
1981-04-13-sts1-red-aurora.context: The red aurora appeared the night Space Shuttle Columbia launched on its first flight (STS-1, 12 April 1981), and some people believed the shuttle had crashed or caused the lights. With Dst -311 nT it was the most intense storm since May 1967; cosmonauts on Salyut-6 also described southern auroras from orbit.
1981-04-13-sts1-red-aurora.effects: Police and other agencies reported the lights interfering with their radio transmissions, and there were many UFO calls. Unusually strong equatorial radio scintillation was recorded at Huancayo (Peru) and Ascension Island.

sightings.seen: Red glow in the night sky late Sunday 12 April local time (~03-08 UT 13 Apr); Los Angeles Times ran the headline 'Aurora borealis lights up sky'; many reported it as a UFO.

sightings.place: Gulf of Mexico coast (Louisiana/Texas; state-level reports, approx. position)
sightings.seen: Red aurora reported across the Southwest and Southeast 'as far south as the Gulf of Mexico' and 'even as far south as Texas'.
Observers in Oregon and Nebraska saw greens, oranges and faint yellows under red-topped curtains.
Colourless moving rays (medium brightness) 02:55-04:40 CEST on 12 April (00:55-02:40 UT), during the first phase of the storm (Kp 7o).

1982-07-14-swedish-railway-storm.name: July 1982 storm (Swedish railway-signal storm)
1982-07-14-swedish-railway-storm.context: This was the strongest storm since 1967 and one of the most intense of solar cycle 21, about 2.5 years after solar maximum; a large proton event and Forbush decrease came before it. Because it happened in midsummer, northern skies were barely dark, so relatively few sightings were recorded.
1982-07-14-swedish-railway-storm.effects: In Sweden, railway traffic lights turned red for no apparent reason on the night of 13-14 July, and 4 transformers and 15 lines tripped in the high-voltage grid; telecommunications were also affected. Modelled field changes near Stockholm exceeded ~2500 nT/min around midnight, several times the ~480 nT/min rate of the 1989 Québec blackout.

sightings.seen: On the night of 13-14 July the aurora was reported directly overhead: 'the strongest auroral surge of the last decade'.
Aurora directly overhead on the night of 13-14 July.
Aurora directly overhead on the night of 13-14 July.
Medium-bright white curtain with rays, 01:00-02:00 CEST 14 July (23:00-00:00 UT), during Kp 9o.
Same display: a white curtain with rays around 23-00 UT, despite the short midsummer night.

1986-02-09-solar-minimum-superstorm.name: February 1986 storm
1986-02-09-solar-minimum-superstorm.context: It was one of the largest storms in 40 years, yet it came only months before solar minimum (Sept 1986) from a series of modest flares on 4-7 February, a reminder that superstorms do not only happen at solar maximum. It peaked as Halley's Comet reached perihelion (9 Feb 1986).
1986-02-09-solar-minimum-superstorm.effects: The magnetosphere was strongly compressed on 8 February, and satellites saw low-energy ions penetrate deep into the plasmasphere (to L~1.2). Ionospheric disturbances were widespread. No specific power-grid or satellite failures were found in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Medium-bright aurora in the early morning of 9 February 1986 (Beck 1986), which would also have been visible from NW Germany.
Intense green aurora (IBC III, 557.7 nm >100 kR) all night in the auroral zone, with none of the dominant red seen in 1989.

1989-03-14-quebec-blackout.name: March 1989 storm (Québec blackout storm)
1989-03-14-quebec-blackout.context: Sunspot region 5395 was one of the most flare-productive ever (X15 flare on 6 March); two CMEs from flares on 10 and 12 March hit Earth in succession. It remains the largest Dst storm of the space age, and some people who had never seen an aurora feared a nuclear attack.
1989-03-14-quebec-blackout.effects: Hydro-Québec's grid collapsed in ~90 s at 07:45 UT (02:44 EST), leaving ~6 million people without power for about 9 hours; later, ~200 grid problems across North America damaged a Salem (NJ) nuclear-plant transformer, and transformers were damaged in the UK and lines tripped in Sweden. GOES imagery was interrupted, TDRS-1 logged 250+ anomalies, satellites crossed outside the magnetopause, and HF radio was disrupted worldwide.

sightings.seen: Aurora seen during the blackout after ~07:45 UT 13 March, unusually clear because the city lights were out.
Around 22-23 CET (21-22 UT) a bright glow behind clouds and three rays reaching the zenith; the display over Germany peaked ~22:00-22:45 UT.

sightings.place: Cuba (country-level report; Havana used as position)
sightings.seen: Aurora sighted as far south as Cuba on the night of 13-14 March, mostly great red patches with little structure over the southern US and Caribbean.
Pale green glow in the south at dusk; by 10 pm NZST (10:00 UT 13 Mar) the arc passed through the zenith, and red and cream rays formed an overhead corona bright enough to cast faint shadows.
Aurora australis observed on the night of 13 March, the farthest-north Australian sighting (about the Tropic of Capricorn).

1989-10-21-october-1989.name: October 1989 storm (X13 flare / great proton event storm)
1989-10-21-october-1989.context: The storm was driven by a very fast CME (~1-day transit) from an X13/4B flare on 19 October in region 5747, one of the most flare-productive regions since 1976. It was the third great storm of the extraordinary year 1989, bringing rare red auroras to Japan and bright displays over northern Europe.
1989-10-21-october-1989.effects: GOES satellites were pushed outside the magnetopause, several satellites in high and low orbits had anomalies, and voltage swings appeared on a Japan-US submarine cable. The X13 flare's proton storm (>10 MeV flux 40,000 pfu) was one of the largest of the space age, with ground-level neutron enhancements, while Space Shuttle Atlantis (STS-34) was in orbit.

sightings.seen: 19:00 UT 20 Oct: a pulsating red curtain up to ~50 deg altitude in the NW with bright rays; at 19:25 UT a greenish patch near Polaris became so bright it cast shadows.
~19:10-19:50 UT 20 Oct: aurora covered 7/8 of the sky, a 'waterfall' up to 75-80 deg with orange waves and white rays fanning from a patch in the SE (corona-like).
Bright red (630 nm, up to ~8.8 kR) aurora low on the northern horizon (0-18 deg elevation) at 11:35-12:30 UT and 14:15-14:25 UT on 21 Oct, with faint green rays.
Red aurora photographed looking north around the 11:37 UT break-up on 21 Oct; almost pure red with a few faint green rays.

sightings.place: Florida, USA (state-level report; approx. central Florida)
sightings.seen: Aurora reported as far south as Florida (Allen 1989), with further reports from Australia; no details available.

1991-03-25-march-1991.name: March 1991 storm (new radiation belt storm)
1991-03-25-march-1991.context: An X9/3B flare on 22 March launched a very fast CME whose shock hit Earth only ~29 hours later, producing an exceptionally sharp, 'anomalous' sudden commencement. The storm is famous among space physicists for creating a new radiation belt almost instantly.
1991-03-25-march-1991.effects: Within about a minute of the 03:42 UT shock, the CRRES satellite saw a brand-new radiation belt of >15 MeV electrons and protons form at L~2-3, which persisted long afterwards. Radiation from the record proton event (>10 MeV peak 43,000 pfu) degraded the GOES-6 and GOES-7 solar panels, cutting GOES-7's expected life by 2-3 years; there were other satellite anomalies and power-grid surges.

sightings.place: 'Scopeville' dark-sky site ~70 miles SW of Kansas City, Kansas (approx. position)
sightings.seen: Around local midnight 23/24 Mar (~06 UT 24 Mar) a pink cast spread across the north, bright white spikes shot toward Polaris, and green, orange, red and yellow patches followed; at peak it stretched east-west to near the zenith for ~2 h.
Aurora seen ~10:45 pm EST Sunday 24 Mar (~03:45 UT 25 Mar); worried residents called the airport thinking it was aliens.
'Very bright', spectacular aurora with a great variety of forms and colours on the night of 24-25 Mar (Sterne und Weltraum 8-9/1991).

1991-11-09-november-1991.name: November 1991 storm (global red aurora)
1991-11-09-november-1991.context: It struck on a clear Friday evening just after new moon, so millions across North America and Europe saw a rare blood-red aurora; AP reported sightings 'from Ohio to Utah and as far south as Texas'. Unusually, it began with bright sun-aligned arcs over the polar cap (Eureka, 89 deg CGM) before the red aurora spread equatorward.
1991-11-09-november-1991.effects: The lights caused a wave of 911, police and radio-station calls across the central US. The storm delivered roughly half the ionospheric energy input of March 1989; no major infrastructure failures were found in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: A 'pinkish, red haze' on Friday night 8 Nov; alarmed citizens called 911 about 'nuclear lights', and a fire truck was sent out.
Strong lights for ~45 minutes, moving from east to north and changing from orange to red; the local radio station got dozens of calls.

Red, green, orange and yellow patches from dusk; an intense white arc raced overhead from east to west, a 60-deg red-orange tower rose in the NW, and activity reached the southern sky near Orion, lasting until nearly dawn.
For ~20 minutes a 'brilliant red dust cloud' swept across the valley from east to northwest.
Night of 8-9 Nov: repeated red rays along the northern horizon; red dominated, and a greenish curtain climbed high as the aurora moved south.

2000-07-15-bastille-day.name: Bastille Day storm
2000-07-15-bastille-day.context: Named after France's national day, when an X5.7 flare erupted on 14 July 2000 and launched a CME at about 1,500 km/s. It came with one of the strongest proton storms of the space age (about 24,000 pfu) and a ground-level cosmic-ray enhancement, and Voyager detected the shock months later in the outer heliosphere.
2000-07-15-bastille-day.effects: The Japanese X-ray satellite ASCA lost attitude control, tumbled and later re-entered (March 2001); SOHO lost about 2% of solar-panel output in a day and Wind about 25% of its transmitter power, and the ISS dropped 10-12 km in altitude. GPS was degraded for hours, and voltage swings and transformer damage were reported at North American power plants (no blackouts).

sightings.seen: Aurora reported despite a full Moon; the southernmost specific US report found (night of 15-16 July local).
Bright red aurora straight overhead (photographed by Ronnie Sherrill); coordinates are a state-level approximation.
The sky blazed white, then green, then red from horizon to horizon.

2001-03-31-march-2001-superstorm.name: March 2001 superstorm
2001-03-31-march-2001-superstorm.context: The storm was driven by a CME from giant sunspot region AR 9393 (X1.7 flare on 29 March). Its Dst of -387 nT was the largest of solar cycle 23 until November 2003, and northern lights were reported as far south as Mexico.
2001-03-31-march-2001-superstorm.effects: This was a G5 (extreme) storm, but a second CME at about 22 UT turned the interplanetary field northward and quenched it, so the whole episode lasted barely 24 hours. That may have spared power grids from damage, and no major infrastructure failures were documented in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Red auroral glow over Houston as the storm spread to southern latitudes (night of 30-31 March local).
Aurora photographed with 20-second exposures, in a place where auroras are very rare.

sightings.place: Sunrise Highway near San Diego, California, USA
sightings.seen: Red aurora photographed behind cirrus clouds (60-s exposure).
Red curtains and green streamers pulsating all across the sky.
Red and green auroras danced for hours; coordinates are an approximate range location at about 37N.

2001-11-06-november-2001.name: November 2001 storm
2001-11-06-november-2001.context: A full-halo CME launched two days earlier by an X1 flare from sunspot AR 9684 hit Earth at about 01:50 UT on 6 November. Vivid red and green auroras were reported from Tennessee, Alabama, the Carolinas, Florida, Texas and California.
2001-11-06-november-2001.effects: This was a severe (G4) storm that lasted more than 24 hours. No specific infrastructure failures were documented in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Red aurora captured in 20-30 s exposures around 2 AM local.

sightings.place: Calaveras Reservoir, San Jose hills, California, USA
sightings.seen: 'Blood-red' aurora over the reservoir.
Around 8 PM PST on 5 Nov (about 04 UT on 6 Nov): 'a solid mass of color, with peach colored beams'.
Skies over central Europe glowed bright red and violet; the coordinates are regional.
Aurora australis photographed with the Southern Cross at 09:45 UT on 6 Nov; the location is approximate (island-level).

2003-10-30-halloween-storms.name: Halloween storms
2003-10-30-halloween-storms.context: Sunspot region 486 fired an X17 flare on 28 Oct and an X10 on 29 Oct, and both CMEs reached Earth in only about 19 hours, producing back-to-back G5 storms. On 4 Nov it produced the largest flare of the GOES era (it saturated the GOES sensor; estimates range from about X28 to X45). Auroras were reported from Texas, Florida and the Mediterranean, as well as Australia.
2003-10-30-halloween-storms.effects: Strong geomagnetically induced currents left about 50,000 customers in Malmö, Sweden without power for up to an hour on 30 Oct, and South African transformers were damaged. The FAA's WAAS GPS augmentation was unusable for about 15 hours on 29 Oct. Over half of Earth-orbiting spacecraft reported anomalies, Mars Odyssey's MARIE radiation instrument was lost, ISS crew sheltered, and polar flights were rerouted at $10k-100k per flight.

sightings.seen: Aurora photographed on 29 Oct 2003 (NASA image), well outside its normal range.
Aurora at about 1 AM local on 29 Oct (about 08 UT); the observer's first ever in Utah.
Aurora display at about 6:45 PM CST on 29 Oct (about 00:45 UT on 30 Oct).
Green and white auroral beams at the zenith on 29-30 Oct (IPS listserver via Love et al. 2025) - the southern-hemisphere counterpart of the US displays.
Aurora photographed from the city during the 30-31 Oct display.

2003-11-20-november-2003-superstorm.name: November 2003 superstorm
2003-11-20-november-2003-superstorm.context: A surprisingly modest eruption on 18 November produced a magnetic cloud with an exceptionally strong field of about 56 nT and a long southward orientation. It drove the largest Dst since March 1989, and none larger has been recorded since.
2003-11-20-november-2003-superstorm.effects: This was the most intense storm of solar cycle 23 by Dst. TIMED/GUVI saw thermospheric O/N2 depletions reaching the equator and strong ionospheric disturbances, with GPS scintillation reported at low latitudes; no major grid failures were documented in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Aurora seen about an hour before local midnight (about 21 UT); the observer wrote that 'the impossible has happened' at Mediterranean latitude.
The sky turned colourful with aurora on the Cantabrian coast and as far south as Valencia; it is one of Spain's few 21st-century auroras.
Aurora visible for several hours, from 7 to 11 PM local (18-22 UT).
Pink shafts of light at the zenith (the highest point of the sky) - the lowest-latitude zenith aurora of the storm (43.7 deg geomagnetic; IPS listserver via Love et al. 2025).
Aurora photographed with an airliner approaching Hartsfield airport; from Ohio, red aurora even appeared in the SOUTHERN sky around Mars.

2004-11-08-november-2004.name: November 2004 storms
2004-11-08-november-2004.context: A burst of late-cycle-23 activity (22 M-class and 3 X-class flares in late October to early November 2004) sent several CMEs Earthward. By Dst it is roughly the tenth-largest storm since 1957.
2004-11-08-november-2004.effects: This was an extended multi-day disturbance with two main dips (Dst -374 nT on 8 Nov and -263 nT on 10 Nov). No specific infrastructure failures were documented in the sources consulted.

sightings.seen: Night of 7-8 Nov local: only brief glimpses through cloud breaks; the glow showed up in photos but not to the eye.
Night of 7-8 Nov local: 'Looked as if the Sun was rising in the North!'
Night of 9-10 Nov local (second storm): the entire northern sky ablaze with a cherry-red glow, easily seen by naked eye.

sightings.place: Duns Creek, New South Wales, Australia
sightings.seen: 10 Nov: a rare aurora australis at about 32S.
A white, pink and green 'grid pattern' of aurora overhead at the zenith (IPS listserver via Love et al. 2025).

2015-03-17-st-patricks-day.name: St. Patrick's Day storm
2015-03-17-st-patricks-day.context: The CME arrived hours earlier than forecast (expected around 12 UT) and the storm grew far stronger than anticipated, becoming the cycle's largest on St. Patrick's Day. Aurorasaurus citizen-science reports showed auroras visible farther equatorward than the OVATION model predicted.
2015-03-17-st-patricks-day.effects: This was the strongest storm of solar cycle 24 (G4). It produced strong high-latitude ionospheric irregularities that degraded GPS, and magnetic declination at Deadhorse, Alaska swung by about 9 degrees. Power grids were not disrupted.

sightings.seen: Aurora photographed at about 3 AM local during the storm night.
Vibrant green aurora already at sunset on 17 Mar.
Aurora seen on the night of 17-18 Mar; reports also came from southern England and Poland, places that rarely see it.

sightings.place: Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia
sightings.seen: Aurora australis photographed the night after the main storm (18 Mar local); it was also seen from Tasmania and from Dunedin, New Zealand.

2024-05-10-gannon.name: Gannon storm (Mother's Day storm)
2024-05-10-gannon.context: Sunspot region AR 13664 launched a train of CMEs that produced the first G5 (extreme) storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. It was named after the late space-weather physicist Jennifer Gannon, and millions of smartphone users photographed auroras from Mexico, the Canary Islands, northern India, Namibia and tropical Queensland, making it perhaps the best-documented low-latitude aurora in history.
2024-05-10-gannon.effects: GPS/GNSS degradation hit precision agriculture (RTK-guided tractors stalled mid-planting, with estimated losses of about US$17,000 per affected farm) and drones. About 5,000 LEO satellites performed the largest orbit-maintenance 'migration' on record, and Starlink service was degraded. Grids held (New Zealand's Transpower took precautionary action) and HF radio was disrupted.

sightings.seen: Naked-eye aurora up to 45 deg elevation (55 deg by camera) with visible structure, at -23.2 deg MLAT; this report sets the reconstructed 29.8 deg ILAT oval boundary.

sightings.place: Chewko Lookout near Mareeba, Queensland, Australia
sightings.seen: Naked-eye aurora australis at -24.2 deg MLAT, among the most equatorward naked-eye reports; nearby Bromfield Swamp saw pinkish-purplish aurora up to 20 deg elevation.
Naked-eye aurora reaching about 60 deg elevation, with pinkish colours and explicit structure (31.0 deg MLAT), giving a 35.5 deg ILAT northern oval boundary.
Aurora low on the northern horizon: about 5 deg elevation by naked eye and 20 deg by camera, at 24.3 deg MLAT.

sightings.place: Mogán, Gran Canaria, Canary Islands, Spain
sightings.seen: Photographed aurora dominated by purplish (nitrogen) rather than red light.

2024-10-10-october-2024.name: October 2024 storm
2024-10-10-october-2024.context: A single fast CME (about 1,200-1,300 km/s) from an X-class flare late on 8 October (US time) triggered a 'super substorm' right after the shock arrived. That pushed red aurora deep into mid-latitudes over Japan and, hours later, across the southern US and Mexico, only five months after the Gannon storm.
2024-10-10-october-2024.effects: The storm raised concerns for power grids already weakened by Hurricane Milton in Florida; no major failures were reported. USGS noted the usual G4 impacts on GPS, satellite operations, HF radio and directional drilling. ESA Swarm data showed a peak magnetic disturbance nearly as strong as May 2024, but it subsided faster.

sightings.seen: Aurora reported as far south as Toa Baja (+18.4N), the southernmost sighting cited in the GOLD vortex study; probably camera-level.

sightings.place: Sugarloaf Key (near Key West), Florida, USA
sightings.seen: Northern lights photographed about 15 miles from Key West; pink, purple, red and green hues were reported across the southern US.
Pink and green aurora photographed on the night of 10 Oct; also reported from Chihuahua, Coahuila, Baja California, Zacatecas and Jalisco. Coordinates are approximate (Hermosillo).
Red and pink aurora australis in the pre-dawn of 11 Oct local, the northernmost Australian report in ABC coverage; seen widely from Tasmania to Sydney and the Adelaide Hills.
Aurora photographed over northeast China; in Japan, red aurora up to about 950 km altitude was photographed widely from 17 UT.

2025-11-12-november-2025.name: November 2025 storm
2025-11-12-november-2025.context: A series of CMEs, followed by the year's strongest flare (X5.1 at 10:04 UT on 11 Nov), hit Earth in quick succession. The overnight aurora of 11-12 November was seen across the US as far south as Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Florida and Mexico.
2025-11-12-november-2025.effects: This severe (G4) storm came close to G5. USGS noted its typical effects on aeromagnetic surveys, directional drilling, satellite operations, GPS and over-the-horizon radio, but no power interruptions.

sightings.seen: Red, pink and purple aurora reported low in the northern sky on the night of 11-12 Nov local; the location is an approximate placeholder (Gainesville).
Vibrant pink, red and green aurora photographed.
Evening of 12 Nov local: purple, blue and green aurora australis seen soon after sunset.
Aurora australis photographed on the night of 12 Nov local.
